question: An admin is configuring Okta Universal Directory to act as the profile source for a user attribute instead of an upstream app. What must be true before that attribute can be set to be 'sourced from Okta' on the Profile Editor mapping?
options: The attribute mapping direction for every app that previously wrote to it must be changed so Okta is the authoritative source and the attribute is no longer overwritten by an inbound app-to-Okta mapping
The attribute must be deleted from every app's profile schema first
The org must disable Universal Directory and re-enable it in single-source mode
The attribute must be marked read-only in the Okta admin console
explanation: Making Okta the source for an attribute means no inbound (app-to-Okta) mapping should overwrite it going forward, so any existing 'apply on every import' mapping from another app must be changed or removed; otherwise the next import cycle overwrites the Okta-sourced value. Deleting the attribute (B) removes the schema field entirely, disabling UD (C) is unrelated and destructive, and read-only (D) would prevent admins/apps from writing it via the intended path.

question: A consultant wants a custom attribute value entered directly in the Okta profile to persist across future imports from the HR-driven app. Which sourcing configuration is required?
options: Set Okta as the profile source ('As a Source') for that attribute so inbound mappings from the HR app do not overwrite it
Enable 'push groups' for the HR app
Turn on JIT provisioning for the HR app
Set the attribute's data type to read-only in Universal Directory
explanation: 'As a Source' designates Okta itself as authoritative for that attribute, which prevents subsequent HR-app imports from clobbering the manually-set value. Push groups (B) is a group feature unrelated to attributes, JIT (C) governs account creation timing, and marking read-only (D) would block Okta admins from editing it themselves too.

question: When multiple apps are assigned to a user and one is configured 'As a Source' for the department attribute, what happens if a second, non-source app also has an inbound mapping for department?
options: The second app's inbound mapping for that attribute is effectively ignored for department because only the designated source app (or Okta) is authoritative for that field
Both apps write simultaneously and the value alternates on each import
Okta throws an import error and blocks provisioning for the user
The second app becomes the new source automatically
explanation: Per-attribute sourcing means only one source (an app or Okta) is authoritative for a given attribute at a time; a non-source app's inbound mapping for that same attribute won't override the sourced value. Values don't 'alternate' (B), this isn't a hard error condition (C), and source designation must be explicitly configured, not auto-assigned (D).

question: An organization sources 'title' from both Workday and Active Directory, with Workday imported nightly and AD imported hourly. Which factor actually determines which value wins for 'title' on the Okta profile?
options: The explicit profile source priority/precedence configured for that attribute in Universal Directory, not which app happens to import more frequently
Whichever app's import job finishes first each day
Alphabetical order of the app names
The app with more total assigned users
explanation: Profile source priority is an explicit, admin-configured precedence per attribute — it is not determined by import frequency, job completion order, naming, or user counts. Options B-D describe incidental factors that have no bearing on Okta's sourcing precedence logic.

question: A consultant needs 'employeeNumber' to always come from the HR system even if a downstream app tries to overwrite it during account linking. What is the correct approach?
options: Configure the HR app as the profile source ('As a Source') for employeeNumber so other apps' inbound mappings cannot override it
Disable account linking entirely for all apps
Set employeeNumber to a static default value in the schema
Remove employeeNumber from every other app's profile mapping page entirely
explanation: Designating the HR app as the source for that attribute is the built-in mechanism for this exact requirement. Disabling account linking (B) is a broader, unrelated control, a static default (C) defeats the purpose of syncing real HR data, and manually stripping the mapping from every other app (D) is unnecessary and unmanageable versus using source priority directly.

question: Which statement correctly describes attribute-level (as opposed to app-level) sourcing in Okta?
options: Different attributes on the same Okta profile can each be sourced from a different app or from Okta itself, independent of one another
Once an app is set as a source, it becomes the source for every attribute on the user profile
Sourcing can only be configured at the org level, applying identically to all attributes and all apps
Attribute sourcing requires SCIM provisioning and cannot be used with SWA or SAML apps
explanation: Sourcing in Okta is granular per attribute — one app can source 'department' while another sources 'manager' and Okta itself sources a custom field. It is not all-or-nothing per app (B), not a single org-wide setting (C), and is independent of the app's specific sign-on protocol (D).

question: During a phased advanced-sourcing rollout, a consultant wants to validate mapping behavior for a small subset of users before enabling it org-wide. What is the recommended testing approach?
options: Scope the app assignment (and therefore the mapping/import behavior) to a limited test group first, verify profile results, then expand assignment to the full population
Enable the mapping for all users immediately and monitor the System Log for errors afterward
Duplicate the entire org into a second tenant for every sourcing change
Test only in the Profile Editor UI without ever running a live import
explanation: Scoping the app/mapping to a pilot group and validating real import results is the standard staged-rollout pattern for sourcing changes, limiting blast radius before a full cutover. Enabling org-wide first (B) risks broad data corruption, duplicating tenants (C) is impractical for routine changes, and the Profile Editor alone (D) doesn't exercise the actual live import pipeline.

question: After changing an attribute's profile source, several existing users still show the old value. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The next scheduled (or manually triggered) import from the new source app hasn't run yet, so profiles haven't been refreshed with the new sourced value
Attribute source changes only apply to newly created users, never existing ones
Universal Directory caches source assignments for 30 days before applying them
The Profile Editor mapping was saved in the wrong app instance
explanation: Sourcing changes take effect on the next import cycle for that source app; until an import runs (scheduled or manually triggered), existing profiles retain their prior values. There's no such 'new users only' restriction (B) or fixed 30-day cache delay (C) in the sourcing model, and while a wrong app instance (D) is possible it's a less likely, more specific misconfiguration than simply awaiting the next import.

question: A consultant is troubleshooting why an attribute value reverted after a source-app import even though it was manually edited in the Okta admin console. What's the root cause?
options: The attribute's profile source is still the app, not Okta, so the next import overwrote the manual edit with the source system's value
The Okta admin console does not support manual attribute edits at all
The user must be deactivated and reactivated for manual edits to persist
Manual edits are always permanent and cannot be reverted by any import
explanation: If the app (not Okta) is still configured as the attribute's source, any manual console edit is a temporary override that the next import will overwrite with the source system's authoritative value — this is expected sourcing behavior, not a bug. The console does support manual edits (B is false), deactivation/reactivation isn't relevant (C), and manual edits are not inherently permanent when a source app still owns the field (D is false).

question: When migrating a large user population from a legacy identity store into Okta with advanced sourcing, which practice reduces risk of mass profile corruption?
options: Validate mappings and run imports against a staged subset first, and reconcile/dry-run attribute diffs before a full cutover
Import the entire population in one batch with no dry run to save time
Manually re-key every user's profile by hand after the migration completes
Disable all profile mastering rules during the migration and re-enable them afterward
explanation: Staged validation and dry-run reconciliation before full cutover is standard migration risk mitigation, catching mapping errors on a small population instead of the whole org. Skipping dry runs (B) maximizes risk, manual re-keying at scale (C) is impractical, and disabling mastering rules (D) removes the very controls meant to keep data consistent during migration.

question: A data migration plan calls for importing historical employee records where some required attributes are missing from the legacy export. What should the consultant do before go-live?
options: Identify and remediate or backfill missing required attribute data in the source system (or via a transformation step) before importing, since Okta will not fabricate missing values
Import anyway and let Okta auto-generate placeholder values for any missing attributes
Make all previously required attributes optional in the Okta schema permanently
Skip importing any user with any missing attribute value and manually create those accounts later with no plan to reconcile
explanation: Data quality issues in the source must be fixed or transformed before import; Okta does not invent values for missing data. Auto-generating placeholders (B) isn't a real Okta migration behavior, permanently loosening required attributes (C) is an overcorrection that weakens data integrity long-term, and skipping affected users with no reconciliation plan (D) just defers the problem.

question: In an HR-as-a-Source deployment (e.g., Workday), what is the primary architectural benefit compared to sourcing user data from Active Directory alone?
options: HR systems typically hold authoritative lifecycle data (hire/term dates, job changes) earlier and more accurately than AD, enabling more accurate automated provisioning and deprovisioning timing
HR-as-a-Source eliminates the need for any profile mappings whatsoever
HR-as-a-Source is required before Okta can support SAML applications
HR-as-a-Source automatically disables all AD import agents
explanation: HR systems are usually the true system of record for employment lifecycle events, so sourcing from HR lets provisioning/deprovisioning react to real hire/term events sooner and more reliably than waiting on AD updates that may lag. Mappings are still required (B is false), SAML support has no such HR dependency (C), and HR-as-a-Source doesn't disable unrelated AD agents (D).

question: With HR-as-a-Source configured, an employee's termination date is entered in the HR system for a future date. What is the expected Okta behavior, assuming standard lifecycle automation is configured?
options: Okta can automate a scheduled deactivation/deprovisioning workflow keyed off the HR termination date once it is imported and mapped to a lifecycle-driving attribute
Okta immediately deactivates the user the moment the future date is entered in HR, regardless of the date itself
Okta ignores termination dates entirely since it only reacts to real-time login failures
The user's Okta account is deleted permanently the instant HR imports the date
explanation: HR-as-a-Source lifecycle automation is typically built around scheduled actions tied to imported dates (e.g., deactivate on/after the termination date), not instantaneous action the moment the date is entered. Immediate deactivation on data entry (B) misunderstands scheduled automation, ignoring dates (C) defeats the point of HR-as-a-Source, and permanent deletion as a default automated action (D) is not standard behavior (deactivation, not deletion, is the typical default).

question: A consultant is asked to source both 'costCenter' and 'manager' from Workday while still sourcing 'department' from Active Directory. What does this require?
options: Attribute-level source configuration in Universal Directory, since sourcing is set per attribute and not per app for the whole profile
Choosing exactly one app as the sole source for the entire profile
Building a custom Okta Workflow to reconcile the two sources manually for every import
Disabling AD import entirely since only one directory source is allowed per org
explanation: This is a textbook case for attribute-level sourcing: each attribute independently points to its own authoritative source app. A single whole-profile source (B) can't satisfy mixed per-attribute requirements, a workflow reconciliation hack (C) is unnecessary when native sourcing does this directly, and orgs can absolutely have multiple directory/HR sources simultaneously (D is false).

question: A profile mapping needs to concatenate an HR system's separate 'firstName' and 'lastName' fields into a single Okta 'displayName' attribute. What accomplishes this?
options: An Okta Expression Language transformation in the attribute mapping (e.g., referencing both source fields in a string expression)
A separate Okta Workflow must be built since mappings cannot perform any transformation logic
Manually re-typing displayName for every user after each import
Renaming the lastName field in the source HR system to displayName
explanation: Profile Editor mappings support Okta Expression Language, which can reference multiple source fields and concatenate/transform them inline in the mapping itself — no separate workflow is required for this common case (making B incorrect). Manual re-typing (C) doesn't scale and isn't automation, and renaming a source field (D) doesn't achieve concatenation of two fields.

question: Which scenario correctly describes a valid use of attribute transformation in a profile mapping, as opposed to simple sourcing?
options: Deriving a normalized 'username' attribute by lowercasing and stripping spaces from an inbound 'Full Name' field using an OEL expression in the mapping
Changing which app is authoritative for an attribute
Renaming an attribute's internal Okta variable name
Assigning a user to a new group based on department
explanation: Transformation refers to manipulating an inbound value's format/content during mapping (like normalizing casing/spacing via OEL) — that's distinct from sourcing (which app is authoritative, option B), schema renaming (C), or group assignment logic (D), which are separate Okta concepts entirely.

question: A custom SAML app requires a signed AND encrypted assertion because the SP mandates confidentiality of attribute values in transit. What must the consultant configure in Okta?
options: Upload the SP's encryption certificate in the app's SAML settings so Okta encrypts the assertion with it, in addition to Okta's own signing key for the signature
Only enable assertion signing, since SAML assertions cannot be encrypted by Okta
Switch the app to OIDC, since SAML does not support encryption
Ask the SP to decrypt on their own using Okta's signing certificate
explanation: Okta signs assertions with its own key by default but requires the SP's public encryption certificate to be uploaded before it can encrypt the assertion for that SP — signing and encryption use different keys/certs. SAML does support encrypted assertions (B is false), switching protocols isn't necessary (C), and decryption requires the SP's own private key, not Okta's signing cert (D).

question: An SP requires the SAML Subject NameID format to be 'urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress' but Okta is sending 'unspecified'. What fixes this?
options: Set the Name ID format explicitly in the app's SAML settings to emailAddress and map it to the correct source attribute
Rename the user's Okta username to include '@' so it is auto-detected as an email format
Ask the SP to accept 'unspecified' format instead
Disable SAML and use SWA for this app
explanation: The Name ID format is an explicit SAML app setting in Okta that must match what the SP expects; it isn't auto-inferred from username formatting (B), and changing SP requirements (C) or dropping to SWA (D, which has no assertion-based Name ID at all) sidesteps the actual fix rather than solving it.

question: A multi-instance SAML deployment needs different Attribute Statements per business unit sharing the same underlying app catalog entry. What Okta feature supports this cleanly?
options: Multiple app instances (one per business unit) each with independently configured SAML attribute mappings
A single app instance with conditional Okta Expression Language branching inside one attribute's mapping value
Group Push, since it can vary attribute output per group
Okta Access Gateway, since it can rewrite SAML attributes on the wire
explanation: Provisioning separate app instances is the standard way to give different populations independently configurable SAML settings/mappings under the same catalog app. A single mapping field's OEL expression (B) can add conditional logic but doesn't cleanly support wholly independent attribute statement sets, Group Push (C) only pushes group objects not SAML attributes, and OAG (D) is for header-based/legacy app access, not SAML attribute customization.

question: A SAML app intermittently fails with 'invalid signature' errors after Okta's signing certificate was rotated. What is the most likely cause?
options: The SP's trust configuration still references the old, now-inactive signing certificate and needs to be updated to the new one
SAML certificates never need to be updated on the SP side after rotation
The user's browser cached an old assertion
The app's ACS URL is misconfigured
explanation: After certificate rotation, every relying SP must update its trusted certificate/metadata to the new cert or signature validation will fail — this is a very common post-rotation SAML issue. Claiming no update is ever needed (B) is false, browser caching doesn't affect server-side signature validation (C), and ACS URL misconfiguration (D) produces a different error class (delivery failure, not signature validation failure).

question: Which scenario correctly requires configuring SAML assertion 'Response' signing in addition to (or instead of) 'Assertion' signing?
options: The SP explicitly requires the entire SAML Response element to be signed, not just the inner Assertion, per its own security requirements
Every SAML integration always requires Response signing regardless of SP requirements
Response signing replaces the need for HTTPS on the ACS endpoint
Response signing is only relevant for OIDC apps, not SAML
explanation: Whether to sign the Response, the Assertion, or both is driven by the specific SP's requirements — Okta supports configuring this per app, and it's not a universal default for every integration (B is false). Signing doesn't substitute for transport security like HTTPS (C), and this setting is SAML-specific, not applicable to OIDC (D).

question: What is the primary purpose of Okta Advanced Server Access (ASA) in an Okta deployment?
options: Providing identity-based, ephemeral-credential access management for SSH/RDP access to Linux and Windows servers, rather than web app SSO
Replacing SAML as the protocol for all web application sign-on
Serving as Okta's on-prem AD import agent
Managing MFA enrollment policies for end users
explanation: Advanced Server Access extends Okta's identity model to infrastructure-level access (servers via SSH/RDP) using short-lived, identity-bound credentials instead of static passwords/keys — a different problem than web app SSO (A vs B), unrelated to the AD import agent's directory sync role (C), and distinct from MFA enrollment policy management (D).

question: A security team wants server access grants that automatically expire and avoid long-lived static SSH keys distributed to engineers. Which capability addresses this?
options: Advanced Server Access's ephemeral certificate-based access, issued per session and tied to the authenticated identity
Standard SAML app assignment to the server's admin console
A long-lived shared service account SSH key rotated quarterly
Okta Access Gateway header injection
explanation: ASA issues short-lived certificates per access session tied to identity, directly eliminating the long-lived static key problem. SAML app assignment (B) doesn't apply to raw SSH/RDP access, a quarterly-rotated shared key (C) is still a long-lived static credential (just rotated less frequently), and OAG (D) addresses legacy web app header-based auth, not server shell access.

question: In an Advanced Server Access deployment, what role do the gateway/server agents typically play?
options: They enforce identity-based access decisions and issue short-lived certificates at the server/gateway level, brokering the connection for the authenticated user
They perform bulk AD group imports into Okta
They act as the SAML Identity Provider for the org
They replace the need for any authentication policy in Okta
explanation: ASA's server/gateway components handle the access brokering and short-lived cert issuance at the infrastructure layer for authenticated identities. AD group import (B) is an entirely separate on-prem AD agent function, Okta itself (not ASA agents) is the IdP (C), and authentication policies still govern the underlying sign-on before ASA access is granted (D is false).

question: Which use case is best suited to Advanced Server Access rather than a standard Okta SAML/OIDC app integration?
options: Granting a DevOps engineer time-bound SSH access to a fleet of Linux production servers
Enabling single sign-on for a company's HR web portal
Federating with a partner company's identity provider
Enforcing MFA on a custom OIDC-based internal web application
explanation: Time-bound SSH access to servers is exactly ASA's use case; the other three (HR web portal SSO, partner IdP federation, MFA on an OIDC web app) are standard web application SSO/federation/policy scenarios handled by regular Okta app integrations and authentication policies, not ASA.

question: A legacy on-prem web application only supports header-based authentication and cannot be modernized to SAML or OIDC. Which Okta capability enables SSO for it?
options: Okta Access Gateway (OAG), which proxies requests and injects the required identity headers after validating the Okta session
Standard SAML app configuration, since all apps eventually support SAML
SWA (Secure Web Authentication) exclusively, since header-based apps require credential replay only
Okta Advanced Server Access, since it manages server-level infrastructure access
explanation: OAG is purpose-built to front legacy header-auth or basic-auth apps that can't be modernized to a federated protocol, injecting headers after Okta validates the session. Not all apps support SAML (B is false), SWA replays form credentials rather than injecting headers (C is a mismatch for this use case), and ASA is for server shell access, not web app fronting (D).

question: When deploying Okta Access Gateway, where does OAG typically sit in the network/request path?
options: As a reverse proxy in front of the legacy application, intercepting requests, validating the Okta-authenticated session, and forwarding with the appropriate headers/cookies to the backend app
Inside the Okta cloud tenant itself, with no on-prem or customer-network component
As a browser extension installed on each end user's machine
As a DNS-level filter with no request interception capability
explanation: OAG is deployed as a reverse proxy (typically on-prem or in the customer's network) sitting in front of the legacy app, which is why it can intercept, validate, and forward authenticated requests. It is not purely cloud-side (B), not a client-side browser extension (C), and does far more than passive DNS filtering (D) — it actively intercepts and rewrites requests.

question: A consultant needs to extend Okta's adaptive MFA and session policies to a legacy app that has no native support for modern auth protocols. What is the OAG-based approach?
options: Front the app with OAG so Okta's authentication policies (including MFA) are enforced at the OAG/Okta session layer before any request reaches the legacy backend
Manually configure MFA inside the legacy application's own settings
Use Okta Workflows to poll the legacy app's login logs and disable accounts after failed MFA
This isn't possible; legacy apps must be rewritten first
explanation: Because OAG sits in front of the app and requires a valid Okta-authenticated session (subject to Okta's policies, including MFA) before forwarding traffic, it effectively extends modern policy enforcement to apps that can't natively support it — no rewrite needed (making D false). Configuring MFA natively in the legacy app (B) usually isn't even an option for these apps, and reactive log-polling (C) is not how OAG enforces access.

question: Which statement about Okta Access Gateway app onboarding is most accurate?
options: OAG requires app-specific configuration (upstream server details, header/cookie rules) since it must know how to talk to that particular legacy backend
OAG works identically for every legacy app with zero per-app configuration required
OAG can only front applications that already support SAML
OAG eliminates the need for Okta authentication policies entirely
explanation: Each fronted app needs its own OAG configuration describing the upstream backend and header/cookie behavior, since legacy apps vary in what they expect. Zero-config for all apps (B) isn't realistic given that variance, OAG specifically targets apps that lack SAML/OIDC support (C is backwards), and Okta's authentication policies still apply at the session layer in front of OAG (D is false).

question: A company wants to retire VPN-only access to an internal legacy app for remote workers while still enforcing Okta sign-on policies. Which combination is appropriate?
options: Deploy OAG to front the app and expose it securely without VPN, relying on Okta's authentication/MFA policies enforced at the gateway for access control
Give every remote worker the app's raw internal IP address with no additional controls
Migrate the app to SWA only, since SWA requires no network changes
Disable authentication entirely to simplify remote access
explanation: OAG is designed for exactly this: exposing a legacy internal app securely to remote users while Okta's policies (not VPN) become the access control layer. Exposing raw internal IPs with no controls (B) is a serious security gap, SWA only replays form credentials and doesn't solve network exposure (C), and disabling authentication (D) is the opposite of the security goal.

question: What is a key difference between Okta Access Gateway and a standard SAML/OIDC app integration?
options: OAG operates at the network/proxy layer for apps lacking modern federation support, while SAML/OIDC integrations rely on the app itself implementing a federation protocol
OAG only supports mobile apps, never web apps
SAML/OIDC apps require no Okta authentication policy enforcement at all, but OAG does
OAG and SAML/OIDC are interchangeable terms for the same feature
explanation: The core distinction is architectural: OAG proxies traffic for apps that can't speak SAML/OIDC themselves, whereas standard integrations depend on the target app natively implementing one of those protocols. OAG targets web apps primarily, not exclusively mobile (B is false), Okta authentication policy enforcement applies broadly, not exclusively to OAG (C is backwards), and the two are distinct mechanisms, not synonyms (D).

question: In an OIDC flow, which Okta-issued token contains identity claims about the authenticated user for the client application to consume?
options: The ID token
The access token
The refresh token
The client secret
explanation: The ID token is the OIDC-specific artifact carrying identity claims (sub, name, email, etc.) about the authenticated user. The access token (B) authorizes API calls but isn't meant for identity claims consumption by the client, the refresh token (C) is used to obtain new tokens without re-authentication, and the client secret (D) is a credential for confidential clients, not a token at all.

question: Which OAuth 2.0 role does Okta play when acting as the authorization server issuing access tokens to a client application on behalf of a resource owner?
options: Authorization Server
Resource Owner
Client
Resource Server (always)
explanation: Okta acts as the Authorization Server, authenticating the resource owner (end user) and issuing tokens to the client. The Resource Owner (B) is the end user, the Client (C) is the requesting application, and while Okta can optionally also act as a Resource Server for its own APIs, that is not its primary/defining role in a general OAuth flow (D).

question: A single-page application (SPA) with no backend server needs to authenticate users via OIDC without exposing a client secret. Which grant type/flow is appropriate?
options: Authorization Code flow with PKCE
Client Credentials grant
Resource Owner Password Credentials grant
Implicit flow, since it is the current recommended best practice for SPAs
explanation: Authorization Code with PKCE is the modern recommended flow for public clients like SPAs that can't securely store a secret, protecting against interception without needing one. Client Credentials (B) is for machine-to-machine auth with no user, Resource Owner Password Credentials (C) requires handling raw user passwords directly (discouraged), and Implicit flow (D) is now considered legacy/discouraged in favor of Authorization Code + PKCE.

question: A backend service needs to call an API on its own behalf with no interactive user present. Which OAuth 2.0 grant type fits this machine-to-machine scenario?
options: Client Credentials grant
Authorization Code grant
Implicit grant
Resource Owner Password Credentials grant
explanation: Client Credentials is specifically designed for service-to-service calls with no end user context. Authorization Code (B) and Implicit (C) both assume an interactive user redirect/consent step, and Resource Owner Password Credentials (D) requires actual user credentials, none of which fit a pure machine-to-machine call.

question: Which statement correctly distinguishes OIDC from plain OAuth 2.0?
options: OIDC is an identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0, adding standardized authentication (the ID token and user info) to OAuth's authorization framework
OIDC and OAuth 2.0 are unrelated, competing protocols
OAuth 2.0 always includes an ID token by default
OIDC replaces the need for access tokens entirely
explanation: OIDC extends OAuth 2.0 specifically to add a standardized authentication layer (ID tokens, userinfo endpoint) on top of OAuth's authorization-focused foundation — they are complementary, not competing (B is false). Plain OAuth 2.0 does not natively define ID tokens (C is false), and OIDC still uses access tokens for API authorization alongside ID tokens (D is false).

question: An organization needs to add MFA to a legacy VPN concentrator that only supports RADIUS authentication, with no SAML/OIDC support. What is the appropriate Okta component?
options: The Okta RADIUS Agent, installed on-prem to bridge RADIUS authentication requests to Okta for primary and/or secondary (MFA) verification
Okta Access Gateway, since it is the only component that supports on-prem deployments
A custom SAML app pointed at the VPN concentrator's admin URL
Okta Advanced Server Access, since VPN access is a server access use case
explanation: The RADIUS Agent specifically bridges RADIUS-speaking infrastructure (VPNs, network devices) to Okta for authentication/MFA, which is exactly this scenario. OAG (B) targets HTTP header-based web apps, not RADIUS protocol devices, a SAML app (C) doesn't apply since the concentrator only speaks RADIUS, and ASA (D) governs SSH/RDP server access, not VPN authentication.

question: Where is the Okta RADIUS Agent typically installed relative to the RADIUS client (e.g., VPN device)?
options: On-premises, positioned to receive RADIUS requests from the network device and relay authentication decisions to/from Okta over an outbound connection
Inside the Okta cloud tenant with no on-prem footprint
On the end user's laptop as client software
Embedded directly inside the VPN device's firmware by Okta
explanation: Like other Okta on-prem agents (AD agent, IWA agent), the RADIUS Agent runs on-premises and communicates outbound to Okta, sitting between the RADIUS client and the cloud service. It is not purely cloud-hosted (B), not installed on individual end-user devices (C), and Okta doesn't embed agents into third-party device firmware (D).

question: A consultant configures the Okta RADIUS Agent for a VPN to require MFA as a secondary factor after the primary AD-backed password check. What does this architecture describe?
options: The VPN device sends the primary auth request through RADIUS; the RADIUS Agent coordinates with Okta to layer MFA on top before granting the final RADIUS Access-Accept
RADIUS Agent replaces the VPN device's need for AD authentication entirely, using only Okta passwords
RADIUS Agent only supports SMS as an MFA factor, no other factor types
MFA cannot be layered onto RADIUS-based authentication under any circumstances
explanation: This is exactly the RADIUS Agent's core capability: layering Okta MFA on top of an existing primary authentication step before the final Access-Accept response is returned to the RADIUS client. It doesn't necessarily replace AD auth (B), it isn't limited to SMS-only factors (C), and MFA-over-RADIUS is precisely what this agent enables (D is false).

question: Which factor primarily determines whether the Okta RADIUS Agent is the right tool for a given remote-access integration?
options: Whether the target device/system's authentication protocol is RADIUS rather than a web-based federation protocol like SAML or OIDC
Whether the organization has more than 500 employees
Whether the app is hosted in the cloud versus on-premises
Whether the app supports SCIM provisioning
explanation: The RADIUS Agent's applicability hinges on the underlying auth protocol being RADIUS (common in VPNs, network gear), not company size (B), cloud-vs-on-prem hosting (C, which is more relevant to OAG/agent placement decisions generally but not the defining RADIUS criterion), or SCIM support (D, which concerns provisioning, not authentication protocol).

question: Users report intermittent SSO failures to a SAML app, and the System Log shows periodic 'clock skew' related assertion validation errors. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The SP's server clock has drifted out of the acceptable tolerance window relative to Okta's assertion timestamps (NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter)
The user's Okta password has expired
The app's ACS URL was recently changed
The user is not assigned to the correct Okta group
explanation: SAML assertions carry time-bound validity windows, so an SP with clock drift outside tolerance will intermittently reject otherwise-valid assertions — a classic clock-skew symptom. Password expiration (B) would produce an auth failure at Okta itself, not a downstream assertion timing error, ACS URL misconfiguration (C) causes consistent delivery failures rather than intermittent timing errors, and group assignment issues (D) would produce consistent 'not assigned' errors, not intermittent timing ones.

question: An OIDC integration fails with 'invalid_redirect_uri' during testing. What should the consultant check first?
options: That the redirect URI configured in the Okta app matches exactly (including scheme, host, path, and trailing slash) what the client application is sending in the auth request
Whether the user has MFA enrolled
Whether the client secret has expired
Whether the app is assigned to the correct Okta group
explanation: OIDC redirect URI matching is exact-string-based; even a trailing slash or http-vs-https mismatch triggers this specific error. MFA enrollment (B) would surface as a different, later-stage error, an expired secret (C) produces a token-exchange error rather than a redirect_uri error, and group assignment (D) affects access grant, not the redirect URI validation step which happens earlier in the flow.

question: A SAML app worked in a sandbox org but fails after promotion to production with a 'Response signature invalid' error. What is a likely cause?
options: The production app instance was configured with (or the SP was given) the wrong environment's Okta signing certificate/metadata
The SP does not support production environments
SAML apps cannot be promoted between orgs under any circumstances
The user's browser needs to be restarted
explanation: Each Okta org (sandbox vs. production) has its own distinct signing certificate and metadata; if the SP trusts the sandbox cert/metadata but is receiving production-signed assertions (or vice versa), signature validation fails. SPs generally do support distinct prod environments (B is false), apps are commonly migrated between orgs with proper reconfiguration (C is false), and a browser restart has no bearing on server-side signature validation (D).

question: Where should a consultant look first to diagnose why a specific user's SSO attempt to an app failed, when the app config itself appears correct?
options: The Okta System Log, filtering by that user and the relevant app sign-on event to see the specific outcome.reason for the failure
The app vendor's public marketing website
The Okta release notes for the current month
The organization's DNS zone file
explanation: The System Log is the authoritative per-event diagnostic source, showing exact outcome/reason detail for a specific user's sign-on attempt. A vendor marketing site (B) has no diagnostic value, release notes (C) describe feature changes rather than user-specific failures, and DNS records (D) are unrelated to an individual authentication failure with correct app config.

question: After enabling a new Authentication Policy rule, an OIDC app begins failing step-up MFA unexpectedly for users who previously signed in without issue. What should be checked first?
options: The specific conditions and factor requirements of the newly added authentication policy rule and its priority/ordering relative to existing rules
Whether the app's client ID was typed correctly
Whether the app supports OIDC at all
Whether the user's device has a valid IP address
explanation: A newly added policy rule's conditions and its evaluation order relative to other rules commonly change which rule (and factor requirement) applies to a given sign-in, making this the first thing to inspect for a sudden behavior change tied to that rollout. A typo'd client ID (B) would break the integration entirely, not just add step-up MFA, whether the app supports OIDC (C) is already established since it was working before, and IP validity (D) is a basic connectivity concern unrelated to policy-driven step-up behavior.

question: A consultant needs to verify that a SAML assertion's attribute values match what Profile Editor mapping should produce, before escalating to the SP as a bug. What is an effective diagnostic step within Okta?
options: Use a SAML tracer/inspector on the browser sign-in flow (or the app's preview) to view the actual assertion XML and compare attribute values against the expected mapping output
Assume the SP is always correct and stop testing on the Okta side
Delete and recreate the app instance without further investigation
Only check the Okta System Log summary line with no deeper attribute inspection
explanation: Directly inspecting the raw SAML assertion (via a tracer tool or Okta's own preview) shows exactly what attribute values were sent, letting the consultant confirm whether the issue is on Okta's mapping side or the SP's parsing side before escalating. Assuming the SP is automatically correct (B) skips necessary verification, recreating the app blind (C) is a destructive non-diagnostic shortcut, and a summary-only System Log check (D) usually lacks the attribute-level detail needed to confirm mapping correctness.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: What is the primary purpose of the Okta Provisioning Platform (OPP)?
options: To provide a standardized, extensible framework for building and running provisioning connectors that create/update/deactivate accounts in downstream apps
To replace Universal Directory as the org's user store
To serve exclusively as Okta's SAML certificate management console
To manage only Okta's own internal employee directory
explanation: OPP is the underlying provisioning connector framework/architecture that powers app account lifecycle actions (create, update, deactivate) across many app integrations. It doesn't replace Universal Directory (B, a separate profile store concept), has nothing to do with certificate management (C), and isn't limited to Okta's own internal use (D).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: A consultant is evaluating why a specific app integration supports 'push new user', 'update user attributes', and 'deactivate' but not 'import users'. What does this indicate about that app's provisioning capability set?
options: The app's provisioning connector (built on OPP) exposes only outbound (Okta-to-app) capabilities, not inbound import capability, and each capability is independently supported per connector
All Okta provisioning connectors must support every capability identically
The app must be reconfigured as a SAML app to gain import support
Import capability is controlled by the end user's browser, not the app connector
explanation: Provisioning connectors expose capability flags independently — an app can support outbound actions without inbound import, since these are built and enabled per-connector, not uniformly across every integration (making B false). Protocol type (SAML vs. provisioning connector) is a separate concern from provisioning capability (C), and import capability is entirely server-side connector logic, unrelated to the browser (D).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: Which statement best describes how OPP-based connectors typically communicate with target applications?
options: Via the target application's own API (often REST/SCIM), translating Okta lifecycle events into the app's native provisioning calls
Exclusively via screen-scraping the app's login page
Only through manual CSV file exchange
Via direct database writes to the app's backend database
explanation: Modern OPP connectors typically call the target app's API (REST or SCIM) to perform provisioning actions. Screen-scraping (B) is not how OPP connectors function, manual CSV exchange (C) describes a different, non-real-time integration pattern, and direct database writes (D) would bypass the app's own business logic and is not how supported connectors are built.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: An app in the OIN doesn't natively support Okta's exact required custom attribute for provisioning. What OPP-adjacent capability lets a consultant extend the mapping?
options: Adding a custom attribute to the app's profile schema in Okta and mapping it via Profile Editor, with Okta Expression Language transformations if needed
Rewriting the app vendor's backend source code directly
Disabling provisioning entirely for that attribute with no workaround
Switching every user to manual account creation to avoid the mapping
explanation: Custom attributes can be added to an app's Okta-side schema and mapped (with OEL transformations as needed) without needing app vendor code changes. Rewriting vendor source (B) is outside the consultant's control and unnecessary, disabling the attribute with no workaround (C) doesn't solve the requirement, and reverting to fully manual provisioning (D) defeats the purpose of automation for a single attribute gap.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: Which OPP capability directly enables automated account deactivation in a downstream app when a user is unassigned or deactivated in Okta?
options: The connector's deprovisioning capability, which is invoked as part of Okta's lifecycle management when the triggering event occurs
Group Push, since it manages group membership only
The Profile Editor mapping direction toggle
The System Log's real-time alerting feature
explanation: Deprovisioning is a specific lifecycle capability of the provisioning connector, invoked on unassignment/deactivation events. Group Push (B) only synchronizes group membership, not account lifecycle state, mapping direction (C) governs attribute flow not lifecycle actions, and the System Log (D) is an audit/reporting tool, not an enforcement mechanism itself.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: A consultant is asked to build provisioning support for an internal app that has no existing OIN integration. What is the appropriate OPP-based path?
options: Build a custom SCIM-based or API-based provisioning integration using Okta's custom app provisioning tools, leveraging the same underlying provisioning platform capabilities as OIN connectors
Wait for Okta to add the app to the OIN catalog with no interim option
Use only manual account creation permanently since custom apps cannot be provisioned
Use Okta Access Gateway to handle provisioning instead of OPP
explanation: Custom (non-catalog) apps can still get provisioning support by building a SCIM or custom API-based integration on the same underlying platform capabilities OIN connectors use — there's no need to wait indefinitely for an OIN listing (B is a poor answer) or resign to permanent manual provisioning (C is false). OAG (D) is a proxy for legacy web access, not a provisioning mechanism.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: Why would an organization configure a Custom Email Domain in Okta?
options: So that system emails (activation, password reset, etc.) sent to end users appear to come from the organization's own domain rather than a generic Okta domain, improving trust and deliverability
To change the domain used for employees' Okta usernames
To enable SAML federation with an email provider
To replace the need for a custom URL domain entirely
explanation: Custom Email Domain specifically governs the sending domain/branding of Okta's transactional emails, improving end-user trust and reducing spam-filtering risk versus a generic Okta sending domain. It does not change usernames (B, a separate identifier concept), isn't a SAML federation mechanism (C), and is independent of Custom URL Domain, which governs the Okta sign-in page URL rather than email (D).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: What must an organization do at the DNS level to complete Custom Email Domain setup and ensure deliverability?
options: Add the DNS records Okta provides (e.g., for SPF/DKIM-style validation) to the organization's domain to prove domain ownership and authorize Okta to send on its behalf
Nothing; Custom Email Domain requires no DNS changes
Point the organization's MX records to Okta's mail servers exclusively
Disable SPF and DKIM on the domain to avoid conflicts
explanation: Okta provides specific DNS records the org must add to prove domain ownership and authorize sending, similar to standard email authentication setup — DNS changes are required (B is false). MX record changes (C) would redirect inbound mail delivery, which isn't what this feature needs, and disabling SPF/DKIM (D) would actively hurt deliverability rather than help it.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: After configuring Custom Email Domain, users report that password reset emails are landing in spam. What should be checked first?
options: Whether the required DNS validation records (domain ownership/authentication) were correctly added and have fully propagated
Whether the app assigned to the user supports SAML
Whether the user's MFA factors are enrolled
Whether Universal Directory is enabled for the org
explanation: Incomplete or unpropagated DNS validation records are the most common cause of deliverability/spam issues after enabling a custom sending domain. App SAML support (B), MFA enrollment (C), and Universal Directory (D) are all unrelated to email deliverability configuration.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: Which is true regarding Custom Email Domain and Custom URL Domain as Okta features?
options: They are independently configurable features addressing different aspects of org branding (outbound email sender vs. the sign-in page URL) and can be enabled separately
Enabling one automatically enables the other
They both require the exact same DNS record types with no differences
Custom URL Domain is a prerequisite for Custom Email Domain
explanation: These are separate, independently configurable branding features — one for email sending domain, one for the org's sign-in URL — and neither is a prerequisite for the other (making B and D false), and they require distinct DNS record setups tailored to their purpose (C is false).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: A global company wants localized 'From' addresses per region (e.g., noreply@us.company.com vs. noreply@eu.company.com) for Okta system emails. What does this require?
options: Configuring and validating a separate Custom Email Domain setup for each distinct sending domain/subdomain needed
A single Custom Email Domain configuration automatically handles all regional subdomains with no extra setup
This is not possible with Okta's email domain feature under any configuration
Only achievable through a fully custom-built external email relay outside of Okta
explanation: Distinct sending domains/subdomains each require their own Custom Email Domain configuration and DNS validation — the feature isn't a single blanket setting extending to arbitrary subdomains automatically (B is false). It's a native Okta capability with proper per-domain setup, not impossible (C) or requiring an external relay (D).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: A company wants to build a fully custom sign-in experience (not Okta's hosted widget) while still using Okta as the identity backend. Which capability supports this?
options: The Okta Authentication API (or Identity Engine's equivalent embedded SDKs), allowing developers to build custom UI while Okta handles the underlying authentication logic
Custom URL Domain, since it changes the visual branding of the hosted widget only
Okta Access Gateway, since it is meant for legacy header-based apps
Group Push, since it controls which groups see custom branding
explanation: The Authentication API (and related embedded SDK approaches) is specifically designed to let developers build a fully custom sign-in UI/UX while delegating authentication logic to Okta. Custom URL Domain (B) only rebrands the hosted widget's URL, not a fully custom UI, OAG (C) targets legacy web apps rather than sign-in UX, and Group Push (D) is unrelated to sign-in UI at all.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: Which consideration is most important when choosing a fully custom Authentication API-based sign-in flow over the standard hosted Okta Sign-In Widget?
options: The team building the custom flow takes on responsibility for UX edge cases (MFA prompts, error states, account recovery) that the hosted widget already handles out of the box
There is no difference in effort between the two approaches
The Authentication API cannot support any MFA factors
Custom flows built on the Authentication API are automatically PCI compliant
explanation: Building directly against the Authentication API means the implementing team must handle many UX states (MFA, errors, recovery flows) that the hosted widget provides pre-built, which is a real engineering tradeoff to weigh (making B false). The Authentication API does support MFA factors (C is false), and no authentication approach automatically confers PCI compliance by itself (D is false, since compliance depends on the whole environment, not just the auth API choice).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: Which Okta deployment model consideration determines whether a company can fully white-label the sign-in experience, including hosting on their own domain and using their own frontend framework?
options: Choosing an Authentication API / embedded SDK-based custom deployment model rather than the redirect-based hosted widget model
Choosing between SAML and OIDC app protocols
Choosing between Group Push and manual group assignment
Choosing whether MFA is required or optional
explanation: Full white-labeling and control over frontend hosting/framework is a deployment-model decision (embedded/API-driven vs. redirect-to-hosted-widget), not a question of app protocol (B), group management (C), or MFA policy (D), which are unrelated axes of configuration.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: A developer calling the Okta Authentication API directly needs to handle a response indicating an MFA challenge is required mid-flow. What should the custom UI do?
options: Prompt the user for the required factor per the API's returned state/factor details, then submit the verification call to continue the authentication transaction
Immediately fail the login and tell the user to contact IT
Silently skip MFA and log the user in anyway
Redirect the user to the Okta hosted widget mid-transaction with no state handoff
explanation: The Authentication API is a stateful transaction; when it returns an MFA-required status, the custom UI must prompt for and submit the appropriate factor to proceed — that handling is exactly the tradeoff of going custom. Failing outright (B) breaks legitimate MFA flows, silently skipping MFA (C) is a serious security bypass, and an unhandled mid-flow redirect to the hosted widget (D) would lose the transaction state and isn't a supported pattern.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: What does the Custom URL Domain feature change for end users?
options: The domain name shown in the browser address bar during Okta sign-in (e.g., login.company.com instead of company.okta.com)
The email sending domain for system notifications
The API base URL used by all provisioning connectors
The default language of the sign-in page
explanation: Custom URL Domain rebrands the visible sign-in URL to the org's own domain instead of the default okta.com subdomain. Email sending domain is a separate feature (Custom Email Domain, B), provisioning connector API base URLs are unrelated internal plumbing (C), and default language is a branding/localization setting unrelated to the URL itself (D).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: What is required at the DNS/certificate level to enable a Custom URL Domain?
options: A CNAME record pointing the custom domain to Okta's provided target, plus a valid TLS certificate for that custom domain (Okta-managed or customer-provided)
No DNS changes; only a setting toggle in the admin console
An MX record pointing to Okta's mail servers
Disabling HTTPS entirely for the custom domain
explanation: Custom URL Domain setup requires a CNAME to Okta's target plus a valid certificate for the custom hostname — DNS and certificate work are both required (B is false). MX records (C) govern mail routing, unrelated to a web sign-in URL, and disabling HTTPS (D) would be a serious security regression, not a requirement.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: After enabling Custom URL Domain, some deep-linked bookmarks to the old okta.com sign-in URL start failing for a subset of users. What is the best remediation approach?
options: Communicate the URL change and, where supported, ensure redirects/aliasing are configured so old links continue to route correctly during the transition period
Immediately disable Custom URL Domain and never revisit it
Tell affected users their accounts have been deleted
Force a full password reset for every user in the org
explanation: A planned transition communication plus supported redirect/aliasing handling is the practical way to manage a URL branding cutover without breaking bookmarked links. Reverting entirely (B) abandons the branding goal unnecessarily, claiming accounts were deleted (C) is factually wrong and alarming, and an org-wide forced password reset (D) is unrelated to a URL change and would be a disruptive overreaction.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: Which combination correctly pairs an Okta branding feature with what it controls?
options: Custom URL Domain -> sign-in page address; Custom Email Domain -> system email sender address
Custom URL Domain -> system email sender address; Custom Email Domain -> sign-in page address
Both features control only the sign-in widget's color scheme
Both features are the same setting under two different names
explanation: Custom URL Domain governs the sign-in page's browser address, while Custom Email Domain governs the sender address of system emails — the pairing in A is correct, and B simply swaps them incorrectly. Neither feature is about color/branding theme (C, a separate customization), and they are two genuinely distinct features, not aliases of one setting (D).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: A company wants to use Okta purely as an MFA layer in front of an existing, separate primary authentication system they are not migrating to Okta. Which model does this describe?
options: MFA as a Service (Okta providing step-up/secondary factor verification without being the primary identity store for that population)
Universal Directory replacing the existing primary auth system
Group Push, since MFA is tied to group membership
Advanced Server Access, since MFA applies at the server layer
explanation: MFA as a Service describes exactly this pattern — Okta layered in purely for factor verification while another system remains the primary authentication authority. Universal Directory (B) would imply full identity migration, which the scenario explicitly avoids, Group Push (C) is a group-sync feature unrelated to this integration pattern, and ASA (D) is for server access credentials, not general MFA layering.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: In an MFA as a Service integration, what typically triggers the call to Okta for factor verification?
options: The existing primary application/system, after validating primary credentials itself, calls out to Okta's API (e.g., via the Authentication API or a factor verification API) to complete secondary verification
Okta silently intercepts network traffic to detect login attempts
The end user manually opens the Okta dashboard and clicks 'verify me' with no application involvement
MFA as a Service requires no integration work at all, it just works automatically for any app
explanation: The primary system integrates deliberately with Okta's API after its own primary auth check to request secondary verification — this requires explicit integration work (making D false). Okta doesn't passively intercept network traffic to detect logins (B), and the flow is application-driven, not a manual disconnected user action (C).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: Which factor types could plausibly be offered through an MFA as a Service integration for a legacy application?
options: Any factor type supported by Okta's factor verification APIs (e.g., push notification, TOTP, SMS), depending on what factors are enrolled and enabled by policy
Only hardware security keys, since software factors are unsupported in this model
Only knowledge-based questions, since Okta cannot verify anything else remotely
No factors, since MFA as a Service is a marketing term with no real functionality
explanation: MFA as a Service can surface whichever enrolled/enabled Okta factor types apply, verified via API — it isn't restricted to hardware keys only (B) or knowledge-based questions only (C), and it is a real functional integration pattern, not just marketing language (D).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: A consultant is asked whether MFA as a Service can enforce Okta's adaptive/contextual policies (like requiring step-up for risky sign-ins) for a third-party primary auth system. What is the accurate answer?
options: Yes, if the integration is built to pass relevant context (e.g., IP, device) to Okta's policy evaluation as part of the verification call
No, contextual policy evaluation is never available outside of full Okta primary authentication
Only if the third-party system is also an official OIN-listed application
MFA as a Service can only ever require a static, non-contextual factor with no adaptive capability
explanation: Adaptive/contextual evaluation can extend into MFA as a Service scenarios when the integration is designed to pass the relevant context to Okta as part of verification — it's an integration design question, not a hard platform limitation (making B and D false). OIN listing (C) is unrelated to whether contextual policy can apply to a given MFA verification call.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: What is a key architectural benefit of using MFA as a Service rather than migrating an entire legacy system's authentication to Okta outright?
options: It allows incremental modernization — adding strong, centralized MFA quickly without the larger scope/risk of a full primary-authentication migration project
It is always cheaper regardless of licensing considerations
It removes the need for any Okta licensing for the affected users
It eliminates the need for any further security review of the legacy system
explanation: The practical value is incremental risk reduction — strong MFA sooner, without the scope of a full migration — which is a genuine architectural/rollout tradeoff (making B, a blanket cost claim, and C, a licensing claim, both unsupported generalizations). It also does not remove the need for a broader security review of the still-in-place legacy system (D is false).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: A company needs to validate a password against a custom, non-Okta-native complexity policy at the moment of registration, before Okta accepts it. Which hook type fits?
options: An Inline Hook (specifically a Password Import Inline Hook or Registration Inline Hook context), which calls an external service synchronously during the Okta flow and can reject or modify the outcome
An Event Hook, since it can synchronously block the registration transaction
A SCIM App Wizard integration, since SCIM enforces password policy
Group Push, since group membership determines password policy
explanation: Inline Hooks are synchronous, called mid-transaction, and can influence the outcome (e.g., reject a password) — exactly what's needed here. Event Hooks (B) are asynchronous, fire-and-forget notifications after the fact and cannot block or alter the triggering transaction, SCIM (C) governs provisioning protocol, not password complexity logic, and Group Push (D) is unrelated to password policy enforcement.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: A team wants to notify an external SIEM system whenever a user is deactivated in Okta, without needing to block or alter the deactivation itself. Which hook type is appropriate?
options: An Event Hook, since it delivers an asynchronous notification of the event without needing to influence the outcome
An Inline Hook, since it must run synchronously to notify external systems
Okta Workflows only, since hooks cannot call external systems at all
A Profile Editor mapping, since it can be configured to call SIEM APIs
explanation: Event Hooks are the correct fit for after-the-fact, non-blocking notifications to external systems like a SIEM. Inline Hooks (B) are meant for synchronous scenarios that can alter the outcome, which isn't needed or desired here, hooks (of either type) absolutely can call external systems — that's their whole purpose (C is false), and Profile Editor mappings (D) are for attribute data flow, not event notification/API calls.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes an Inline Hook from an Event Hook?
options: Inline Hooks run synchronously within an Okta transaction and can alter its outcome; Event Hooks run asynchronously after an event has already occurred and cannot alter it
Both hook types are synchronous and can alter transaction outcomes identically
Both hook types are asynchronous notifications with no ability to affect Okta at all
Inline Hooks are for provisioning only; Event Hooks are for authentication only
explanation: The synchronous/blocking-and-can-modify vs. asynchronous/notify-only distinction is the fundamental difference between these two hook types. Claiming both are synchronous (B) or both are non-influential async notifications (C) collapses this real distinction, and the use-case split in D is an oversimplified and inaccurate generalization — both hook types support multiple use cases beyond that narrow split.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: A consultant sets up a Token Inline Hook to add a custom claim to an OIDC access token based on an external system lookup. What must the external service endpoint do?
options: Respond synchronously, within Okta's timeout window, with a correctly formatted response the Inline Hook contract expects, including the commands to add the custom claim
Respond asynchronously at any time in the future with no timeout constraint
Return an HTML page for the end user to view
Nothing; token claims cannot be customized via hooks
explanation: Inline Hooks require a fast, synchronous, correctly-shaped JSON response within Okta's timeout or the transaction fails/falls back per configuration — asynchronous or delayed responses (B) don't fit the inline contract. The external service returns structured data for Okta to process, not an HTML page for a person to view (C), and token claim customization via hooks is a real, supported capability (D is false).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: An Inline Hook's external endpoint becomes unreachable during a live authentication attempt. What is the general expected behavior, assuming no special fallback handling is configured?
options: The Okta transaction that depends on the hook's response fails or is blocked, since the hook could not return the required synchronous decision in time
Okta silently ignores the hook and proceeds as if nothing happened
The end user's account is automatically deleted
Okta falls back to email verification automatically with no configuration needed
explanation: Because Inline Hooks are a required synchronous dependency in the transaction path, an unreachable/timed-out endpoint generally causes that step of the transaction to fail (unless specific fallback handling has been explicitly designed and configured) — Okta does not just silently proceed by default (B), certainly does not delete accounts as a fallback (C), and does not auto-substitute an unrelated verification method with zero configuration (D).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: Which use case is best solved with a Registration Inline Hook rather than an Event Hook?
options: Enforcing custom eligibility/validation logic that must approve or reject a self-service registration attempt before the account is created
Sending a welcome email notification after an account has already been created
Logging registration events to an external analytics dashboard after the fact
Archiving old, already-deactivated user records nightly
explanation: Blocking/validating a registration decision before account creation requires a synchronous Inline Hook that can alter the outcome. The other three examples (welcome email after creation, after-the-fact analytics logging, and a scheduled archival job) are all after-the-fact or scheduled actions better suited to Event Hooks or separate automation, not a blocking inline check.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: What is the primary purpose of Okta's SCIM App Wizard?
options: To let admins configure SCIM-based provisioning for a custom app by specifying the app's SCIM base URL, authentication, and supported schema/operations through a guided UI, without writing a full custom OIN connector
To replace SAML entirely as Okta's only supported sign-on protocol
To convert any REST API into a SCIM endpoint automatically with zero app-side changes
To manage Okta's own internal user schema exclusively
explanation: The SCIM App Wizard is a guided configuration UI for pointing Okta at a SCIM-compliant app endpoint and defining supported operations/schema, without building a bespoke connector from scratch. It doesn't replace SAML (SSO and provisioning are separate concerns, B), it configures Okta to talk to an app that already exposes SCIM — it does not retrofit arbitrary non-SCIM REST APIs into SCIM compliance (C), and it targets external app provisioning, not Okta's own internal schema management (D).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: Before configuring an app in the SCIM App Wizard, what must already be true about the target application?
options: It must expose a SCIM-compliant API endpoint (base URL, supported resource types like Users/Groups, and authentication) that Okta can connect to
It must already be listed as a certified OIN integration
It must support SAML as well as SCIM
It must be hosted exclusively on-premises
explanation: The wizard connects Okta to an app's existing SCIM endpoint, so the app must already implement SCIM — it is specifically useful for apps that are not yet a certified OIN listing (making B backwards), doesn't require SAML support in addition (C, since SCIM is a provisioning protocol independent of sign-on protocol), and works for cloud-hosted apps just as well as on-prem (D is false).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: A SCIM App Wizard integration fails to create users in the target app with a 400-level error referencing an unsupported attribute in the payload. What is the likely fix?
options: Adjust the SCIM App Wizard's attribute mapping/schema configuration to only send attributes the target app's SCIM schema actually supports
Switch the app to SAML-only with no provisioning
Increase the app's assigned license count
Restart the Okta AD agent
explanation: A 400 error citing an unsupported attribute typically means the outbound SCIM payload includes a field the target schema doesn't recognize, fixed by adjusting the wizard's mapping/schema config to match what the app actually supports. Removing provisioning (B) avoids rather than fixes the issue, license count (C) is unrelated to a schema validation error, and the on-prem AD agent (D) has nothing to do with a cloud SCIM app's schema validation.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: Which SCIM operations would a consultant typically enable through the SCIM App Wizard to support full lifecycle management for an app?
options: Create, update/replace, and deactivate (or delete) user operations, plus optionally group operations, matching what the target app's SCIM API supports
Only 'read' operations, since SCIM apps are import-only by design
Only 'delete' operations, since create/update are handled by Universal Directory directly
SCIM operations cannot be selectively enabled; all or nothing
explanation: Full lifecycle support typically means enabling create, update, and deactivate/delete (and optionally group) operations as supported by the target's schema — SCIM apps are not import-only (B is false), Universal Directory doesn't perform the outbound SCIM calls itself (C is false), and the wizard does allow selectively enabling supported operations rather than an all-or-nothing switch (D is false).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: A consultant needs to troubleshoot why group memberships aren't syncing to a SCIM-provisioned app even though user accounts are created correctly. What should be checked first?
options: Whether group push/provisioning and the group SCIM operations are enabled and correctly mapped for that app, since user and group provisioning are configured independently
Whether the app supports SAML single sign-on
Whether the AD import agent is online
Whether the user has enrolled in MFA
explanation: User provisioning succeeding while group sync fails points to group-specific SCIM operations/mapping not being enabled or configured, since these are independent settings within the same app integration. SAML support (B) is unrelated to SCIM group sync, the on-prem AD agent (C) is irrelevant to a cloud SCIM app's group sync, and MFA enrollment (D) has no bearing on provisioning/group sync behavior.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: Which best describes the relationship between the SCIM App Wizard and Okta's broader provisioning platform (OPP)?
options: The SCIM App Wizard is a guided, no-code configuration surface built on top of the same provisioning platform capabilities that power certified OIN connectors
They are entirely unrelated systems with no shared architecture
The SCIM App Wizard replaces OPP entirely for all future app integrations
OPP only supports SAML apps, and SCIM App Wizard is a completely separate protocol stack
explanation: The wizard is a user-facing configuration layer over the same underlying provisioning platform architecture, making custom SCIM integrations accessible without a bespoke connector build — they are related, not unrelated systems (B is false), the wizard supplements rather than replaces OPP for OIN-built connectors (C is false), and OPP is not SAML-specific — provisioning and SSO protocols are separate concerns entirely (D is false).

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: A consultant needs the Custom URL Domain's certificate to be renewed automatically rather than manually tracked. What option addresses this?
options: Using Okta-managed certificate provisioning for the custom domain (where available) so Okta handles renewal, instead of uploading and manually tracking a customer-provided certificate
There is no way to avoid manual certificate tracking for Custom URL Domain
Switching to HTTP-only to avoid certificates entirely
Disabling Custom URL Domain and using Custom Email Domain instead
explanation: Where Okta-managed certificate provisioning is available for a custom domain, Okta handles the renewal lifecycle automatically, removing the manual tracking burden of a customer-provided certificate — so manual tracking isn't the only option (B is false). Dropping to HTTP-only (C) would be a serious security regression and isn't a real option for a sign-in domain, and Custom Email Domain (D) is an unrelated feature that doesn't address sign-in URL certificates at all.

domain: Implementing Custom Configuration Options with Okta
question: An org migrating to a Custom URL Domain wants zero end-user disruption during the cutover. What is a sound rollout practice?
options: Validate DNS and certificate configuration in a staging/test window, confirm the custom domain resolves and authenticates correctly, and communicate the change before fully cutting traffic over
Change the domain instantly in production with no validation and address any issues reactively
Require every user to manually re-enter their password before the cutover for unrelated reasons
Disable the org's existing okta.com URL before the custom domain is confirmed working
explanation: Validating DNS/certificate readiness ahead of time and communicating the change is standard low-risk cutover practice for a sign-in URL change. Cutting over instantly with no validation (B) risks an outage, an unrelated forced password reset (C) doesn't address URL cutover risk at all, and disabling the old URL before the new one is confirmed working (D) risks locking out all users if something is misconfigured.

question: A company has two AD domains within a single forest, each with users needing Okta access. What is the recommended agent architecture?
options: Deploy an Okta AD agent per domain (or a domain-aware agent configuration covering both domains) so Okta can query and import from each domain properly
Deploy a single agent and manually copy user data between domains beforehand
Merge both AD domains into one before Okta integration is possible
Use only LDAP interface with no AD agent, since agents don't support multi-domain forests
explanation: Multi-domain AD integration typically requires agent coverage/awareness per domain so each domain's directory can be properly queried and imported. Manually copying data (B) isn't real integration, forest/domain merging (C) is a drastic and unnecessary prerequisite, and AD agents do support multi-domain forest topologies when properly deployed (D is false).

question: In a multi-forest AD environment with no trust relationship between forests, what does a consultant need to plan for?
options: Separate, independent Okta AD integrations (agent deployments and configurations) per forest, since there's no cross-forest trust to rely on for a unified query path
A single agent that automatically bridges untrusted forests with no additional configuration
Disabling one forest entirely since Okta cannot integrate with multiple forests
Relying on DNS alone to resolve cross-forest authentication with no agent involved
explanation: Without a trust relationship, each forest needs its own independent integration path since there's no native cross-forest query mechanism to lean on. A single agent can't magically bridge untrusted forests with zero configuration (B), Okta does support integrating with multiple forests, not just one (C is false), and DNS resolution alone doesn't substitute for the actual authentication/directory integration mechanism (D).

question: Users in Domain B intermittently fail to import while Domain A imports reliably, in a multi-domain AD integration. What should be checked first?
options: Whether the agent instance/configuration responsible for Domain B has proper connectivity, service account permissions, and is online, independent of Domain A's healthy status
Whether Domain A's agent needs to be restarted, since domains share one health status
Whether Universal Directory is disabled org-wide
